Homer. The ancient Greek poet credited with composing the Iliad and Odyssey, the two foundational epics of Western literature. Living in the eighth century BCE, though precise dates are disputed, Homer is the earliest canonical author in the Western tradition, and the voice through which Greek mythology and Mycenaean civilization reached posterity. Whether Homer was a single historical person or a composite of oral poets remains debated.

Homer composed or compiled the Iliad, an epic of roughly twenty-four thousand lines recounting the final year of the Trojan War, centered on the wrath of Achilles. It is the oldest surviving work of Greek literature and among the oldest in all of European culture. He authored or inspired the Odyssey, a narrative of Odysseus's ten-year return voyage after Troy's fall, balancing adventure, divine intervention, and the domestic yearning for home, what the Greeks called nostos. Homer likely composed his works orally and for oral performance, using formulaic epithets like "swift-footed Achilles" and "wine-dark sea" to aid memory and rhythm, with writing perhaps coming later.

Homer presented the Olympian gods—Zeus, Athena, Apollo—as powerful, capricious, and intimately involved in human affairs, establishing the mythological framework that shaped all subsequent Greek culture. He immortalized Mycenaean civilization of the Late Bronze Age around twelve hundred BCE, though Homer wrote centuries later, making him the chief source for how ancients imagined their heroic past. The epics establish narrative patterns that persist: the hero's journey, the homecoming, the tragic flaw, divine favor and wrath, the roll-call of warriors, and the tension between fate and individual agency. Homer became the basis of Greek education, with young Greeks memorizing and studying his works as the supreme literary authority and moral teacher. The Iliad is his greatest work and the model for all later epic poetry. The Odyssey is the homecoming epic, a narrative of suffering, disguise, and divine protection on the path to restoration. Through these works, the Trojan War became the historical and mythological event that frames all of Greek mythology.
